title: A Sporting Chance
author: Matthew Evans
summary: Matthew Evans asks whether Ofsted is inspecting school standards or school effectiveness, arguing that the confusion between the two drives much of the controversy over inspection and context. Using the Paralympics as a metaphor, he explains that absolute standards ignore context while effectiveness depends on it, so progress and value-added measures are the fairest guide to how well a school does its job. He argues that the new framework's language of expected and strong standard rewards schools that meet an absolute benchmark rather than those doing excellent work in difficult circumstances. Evans then separates the domains: behaviour and safeguarding should be judged against absolute minimum standards by inspectors on site, while attendance, inclusion and achievement need contextualised judgement. He closes by calling for different language for different constructs, so that grades are interpreted as intended.
points: Absolute standards and school effectiveness are different constructs, and conflating them leads people to read an attainment-based grade as a verdict on how well a school teaches.
Progress and contextualised progress measures are the fairest way to judge effectiveness, while attainment thresholds still matter because of real-world consequences for pupils.
Behaviour and safeguarding should be judged against minimum standards that do not bend to context, and this needs inspectors visiting schools rather than data alone.
Attendance and inclusion should be assessed mainly for effectiveness, since many attendance factors lie outside a school's control.
Ofsted should stop using one rubric and one vocabulary for fundamentally different constructs, grading some things and describing others.
quotes: If Ofsted is judging school standards, context is irrelevant. If it is judging school effectiveness, context is everything. The problem comes when they do the former but it is interpreted as the latter.
However, absolute measures are not reliable in telling us about school effectiveness because they ignore context.
The use of the word standard suggests we are in the Olympics, not the Paralympics.
A school could be highly effective in its process whilst, due to school context, never achieve a benchmark outcome.
The new framework appears to be rewarding schools who meet an absolute standard rather than those who are doing great work in a difficult context.
There is no room to make allowance for context when it comes to minimum standards of behaviour and safeguarding.
We can grade some things and describe others. We can present absolute comparative data alongside contextualised success.
The rubric should serve the intent, not just look pretty on a dashboard.
